title: User Stories with Acceptance Criteria
description: The user story is the smallest unit of work that survives contact with engineering, QA, and a stakeholder all at once. Get the shape right and the rest of the sprint follows. Get it wrong and you'll re-write it four times.

worked_examples.title: Forgot-password flow
worked_examples.content_md:
## User story

**As a** customer who has forgotten their password,
**I want** to reset it without contacting support,
**so that** I can get back into my account today rather than tomorrow.

## Acceptance criteria

**Given** I am on the sign-in page and have entered no password,
**When** I tap "forgot password" and enter my registered email,
**Then** I receive a reset link at that email within 60 seconds, valid for one hour.

**Given** I receive the reset link,
**When** I open it within the hour and enter a new password meeting the password rules,
**Then** my password is updated and I am signed in.

**Given** I open the reset link more than one hour after it was sent,
**When** I attempt to use it,
**Then** I see a message that the link has expired, with a clear path to request a new one.

**Given** I enter an email address that is not registered,
**When** I submit the form,
**Then** I see the same confirmation message as if the email were registered — no information is disclosed about whether the email exists in our system.

## Notes

- Dependencies: transactional email service (existing). Rate limiting on reset requests per IP per hour.
- Out of scope: SMS-based reset; security-question fallback; manual reset by support.
- Engineer questions: do we burn the token immediately on first use or allow re-use until expiry? Recommend burn-on-use.

annotations.note: The "so that" line is the one that gets cut for word count. Don't cut it — it's the line that explains to engineering why the edge cases matter.
Notice that every Given/When/Then is independently testable. QA can run them one at a time. If you can't write the test, the criterion is unclear.

The fourth criterion — registered vs unregistered email — is a security requirement that almost always gets missed when stories are written purely from the user's perspective. Audit your stories for these.
Explicit out-of-scope items at the story level prevent scope creep at sprint planning. "Out of scope: SMS-based reset" stops the inevitable "oh, can we just add SMS" mid-sprint.

common_mistakes: Acceptance criteria written as feature descriptions rather than behaviours. "The system has a forgot-password link" is not a criterion; "when I tap forgot-password, X happens" is.
Multiple behaviours bundled into a single Given/When/Then. If the criterion has the word "and" in the Then clause, it's two criteria.
Edge cases missed because the story focuses on the happy path. For every story, ask: what does the unregistered user see, what does the expired link do, what does the rate-limit case look like.
User stories that smuggle in implementation. "As a user, I want OAuth so I can…" is bound to a solution. The user wants to sign in without remembering a password — the team chooses OAuth.
variant_patterns: Discovery variant: skip acceptance criteria entirely; instead document the open questions and the experiments that would close them. Useful in the first two weeks of a feature.
Spike variant: use a story shape but flip the "so that" to learning value — "so that we know whether to commit to approach X". Always time-boxed.
